Prescriptions per 1,000 member-months dropped 18.6% (95% CI [-20.8%, -16.2%]) from a pre-period mean of 12.094 to 9.846, with the decline appearing abruptly in 2024Q3, the first post-policy quarter. GLP-1 spending per member per month fell 16.6% (CI [-19.4%, -13.8%]), driven by lower utilization per member rather than price. This is a pre/post association, not proof of causation: no comparison state or control series was available, and provisional 2025Q3–2025Q4 data were excluded.

arguments.summary: Eastvale's GLP-1 prior authorization requirement took effect 2024-07-01, not 2024-06-01. The original June 1, 2024 date in Provider Bulletin 2024-07 was postponed and superseded by Bulletin 2024-11, and the current authoritative source (EV-MAN-2024-PH, provider manual) confirms 2024-07-01. Critically, claims with dates of service before 2024-07-01 do not require PA, so the clean pre/post split for the utilization comparison is at 2024-07-01; using the superseded June 1 date would misclassify June 2024 services as post-policy.

findings.statement: Authoritative effective date for EV glp1_prior_auth is 2024-07-01, resolved from EV-MAN-2024-PH (provider manual, highest-authority current source); no unresolved conflicts reported.

The earlier effective date of 2024-06-01 (from provider bulletin EV-BUL-2024-007, published 2024-05-15) is superseded by EV-BUL-2024-011 (published 2024-06-10) and must not be used as the policy start date.
EV-BUL-2024-011 states the GLP-1 PA requirement 'now takes effect July 1, 2024' and that claims for GLP-1 agonists with dates of service before July 1, 2024 do not require PA. [EV-BUL-2024-011#p1]

EV-MAN-2024-PH Chapter 5 lists the PA criteria effective 2024-07-01: (1) type 2 diabetes with A1c >= 7.0 after metformin trial, or (2) BMI >= 35 with a documented weight-related comorbidity; approvals last 12 months. [EV-MAN-2024-PH#p1]

The superseded bulletin EV-BUL-2024-007 had required PA for all GLP-1 receptor agonists with a documented type 2 diabetes diagnosis or qualifying weight-management criteria, scheduled for 2024-06-01. [EV-BUL-2024-007#p1]

Searches for transition-of-care / grandfathering / reauthorization provisions for existing GLP-1 prescriptions returned no EV-specific passage; only the date-of-service rule (pre-2024-07-01 claims exempt from PA) is documented.

caveats: The 2024-06-01 date appears in a still-retrievable bulletin; any analyst or automated pipeline keying on the first published date will use the wrong cut point.
June 2024 straddles the postponed launch: services dated on/after 2024-07-01 are the true post-PA regime, and Bulletin 2024-011 exempts services before that date.

No EV policy text was found on whether already-authorized or in-flight prescriptions were grandfathered at launch or on renewal/recertification volume effects; a claims dip at 2024-07-01 could reflect documentation lag rather than reduced prescribing.
Approvals are 12 months, so the first renewal cohort would fall around mid-2025 — relevant if the data window extends that far.
Federal passages retrieved (42 CFR 430.20, 42 CFR 456.703) are general SPA effective-date and DUR rules and do not establish Eastvale's specific PA rules; they were not relied on.

arguments.summary: Eastvale GLP-1 prescribing dropped materially after the prior authorization requirement took effect on 2024-07-01 (the authoritative date from EV-MAN-2024-PH, not the superseded 2024-06-01): prescriptions per 1,000 member-months fell 18.6% from a pre-period mean of 12.094 to 9.846 post, with bootstrap 95% CI [-20.8%, -16.2%] — significant and material at the 5% threshold. The level shift is abrupt and starts exactly in 2024Q3 (12.21 in 2023Q3 and 12.45 in 2024Q2 → 9.79 in 2024Q3), consistent with a policy-timed change rather than a gradual trend. Spending tells the same story but is not care: GLP-1 spend PMPM fell 16.6% (CI [-19.4, -13.8]), and decomposition of the 2024Q2→2025Q2 drop (-17.8%) attributes 113% of the change to utilization per member (-19.9%) while price per prescription actually rose 2.8% and enrollment was essentially flat (-0.1%). This is a pre/post association, not proof of causation — no comparison state, no control group, and 2025Q3–Q4 are provisional and excluded.

findings.statement: Authoritative EV GLP-1 prior authorization effective date is 2024-07-01 (EV-MAN-2024-PH provider manual); the 2024-06-01 date in EV-BUL-2024-007 is superseded by EV-BUL-2024-011, which exempts services dated before 2024-07-01, so the clean pre/post cut is 2024-07-01. [EV-MAN-2024-PH#p1] [EV-BUL-2024-011#p1]
EV data coverage: 2023Q1–2025Q2 are final; 2025Q3 and 2025Q4 are provisional (claims lag) and were excluded from all comparisons; 12 suppressed rows exist in EV GLP-1.

GLP-1 prescriptions per 1,000 member-months fell 18.6% after 2024-07-01: pre-period (2023Q3–2024Q2) mean 12.094 vs post-period (2024Q3–2025Q2) mean 9.846, bootstrap 95% CI [-20.8%, -16.2%], verdict significant_and_material at 5%.
The decline is a discrete level shift beginning in 2024Q3: 12.214 rx/1,000 MM in 2023Q3 and 12.450 in 2024Q2 (the last pre-policy quarter) drop to 9.792 in 2024Q3, the first post-policy quarter.

Raw quarterly GLP-1 volume: prescriptions peaked at 18,508 (2023Q3) and 18,467 (2024Q2), then stepped down to 14,767 (2024Q3), 15,000 (2024Q4), 14,257 (2025Q1), 14,770 (2025Q2); enrollment was stable at roughly 1.48–1.51M member-months throughout, so counts alone do not explain the drop.
GLP-1 reimbursement per member per month fell 16.6% (pre mean $11.295 → post mean $9.423, 95% CI [-19.4%, -13.8%]), significant and material.

Spending fell less than volume because price per prescription rose slightly: spend per Rx went from $933.906 pre to $957.075 post, +2.5% (CI [1.0%, 4.0%]), significant but immaterial at the 5% threshold — the reduction came from fewer prescriptions, not cheaper ones.

Spending decomposition 2024Q2→2025Q2: total GLP-1 spending fell 17.8% ($17.45M → $14.34M), driven by utilization per member (-19.9%, 113.1% of the change) while price per Rx added +2.8% and enrollment was flat (-0.1%).

Sensitivity check using the superseded 2024-06-01 date yields -17.9% (CI [-19.8%, -16.1%]), i.e. the same direction and materiality but it excludes 2024Q2 from the pre-period and drops it as mixed; the 2024-07-01-based result (-18.6%) is the one to report.

All suppressed rows are small-cell exenatide injection figures (NULL, not zero) in every quarter, so GLP-1 totals are complete for the non-suppressed products and no suppressed value was imputed as 0.

caveats: Uncontrolled pre/post comparison: no comparison state, control group, or interrupted-time-series model, so secular market trends in GLP-1 use cannot be separated from the PA requirement.
2025Q3 and 2025Q4 are provisional (claims lag) and were excluded; conclusions hold only through 2025Q2.

arguments.summary: I used **January 1, 2024** as the break point because that is the effective date of State Plan Amendment NL-SPA-2023-014, the highest-authority source (federally approved SPA, no superseding document) [NL-SPA-2023-014#p1]. Northland GLP-1 use rose sharply and immediately after that date: from 11.83 Rx per 1,000 member-months pre to 16.42 post, +38.8% (95% CI 36.4–41.0), a significant and material change judged against a 5% materiality threshold (E2, E5). The Feb 1, 2024 provider-manual date gives an almost identical result (+37.8%, CI 35.8–39.6), so the finding is robust to that conflict (E6). GLP-1 spending per member rose 42.4% (E7), but decomposition shows 91.2% of the spending increase came from utilization per member and only 8.4% from price (E8; per-Rx spending +2.6%, immaterial at E9) — this is more prescriptions, not more expensive prescriptions. Verdict: significant, material, and policy-timed, but this is a pre/post association, not a causal effect.

findings.statement: Break point used: 2024-01-01, the SPA NL-SPA-2023-014 effective date (resolved key, no superseded versions). The SPA amends Northland's outpatient drug benefit to cover GLP-1s for chronic weight management in adults with BMI >= 30, or BMI >= 27 with a weight-related comorbidity; T2D coverage unchanged. Primary metric = prescriptions per 1,000 member-months, so enrollment changes cannot masquerade as utilization.

The step change is visible in raw quarters, not just summary means: 2023Q4 = 11.811 per 1,000mm (10,670 Rx / 903,358 member-months) then 2024Q1 = 16.671 (15,079 Rx / 904,490 member-months), i.e. +41.3% in the first post quarter, with no pre-period trend break beforehand (2023Q1 10,830 Rx; 2023Q4 10,670 Rx).
SPENDING: GLP-1 spend per member per month rose 10.889 -> 15.503 USD, +42.4% (95% CI 40.1–44.6), significant_and_material.

SPENDING DECOMPOSITION 2023Q4 -> 2024Q4: total spend 9,943,049.89 -> 14,152,242.14 USD (+42.3%). Share of change: utilization per member 91.2%, price per Rx 8.4%, enrollment 0.4%. The increase is driven by more people getting GLP-1s, not by higher prices or enrollment growth.

Consistent with the decomposition, spend per Rx was 920.165 -> 944.165 USD, +2.6% (95% CI 1.3–4.0): statistically significant but immaterial (verdict significant_but_immaterial), so price is not the story.
Utility persisted rather than decaying: 2025Q1 Rx per 1,000mm = 16.216 (14,518 Rx / 895,306 member-months), +36.1% vs 2023Q4 and essentially flat vs the 2024 post-period mean of 16.42.

findings.statement: Total SP GLP-1 reimbursement rose 13.1%, from $6,772,662.07 in 2023Q4 to $7,656,893.90 in 2025Q2.

Spending decomposition: enrollment contributed +15.7% (118.8% of the change), price per prescription +5.7% (45.3%), and utilization per member -7.6% (-64.1%) — i.e., the spending increase is entirely an enrollment effect offset by lower per-member volume.
Prescriptions per 1,000 member-months fell from 12.374 in 2023Q4 to 11.438 in 2025Q2, a -7.56% decline, while member-months grew 15.69% (599,829 to 693,940).
Spending per member per month fell 2.28% over the same endpoints ($11.29 to $11.03), so per-member cost was not the driver either.

Trend check around a 2024-07-01 split (used only as a breakpoint, not a Southport policy): utilization per 1,000 member-months pre 12.116 vs post 11.690 = -3.5% (95% CI -6.1% to -0.8%), verdict significant_but_immaterial at a 5% materiality threshold; spend PMPM pre 11.241 vs post 11.252 = +0.1% (95% CI -2.6% to +3.0%), verdict no_meaningful_change. 2024Q3 excluded as missing.

There is no product-mix shift to explain the price component: semaglutide/dulaglutide/liraglutide prescription shares are flat at ~60%/30%/10% in every quarter, so per-Rx price growth comes from within-product price increases (semaglutide $913.72 → $956.70, dulaglutide $905.26 → $978.88 from 2023Q4 to 2025Q2).

Data quality: SP quarters 2023Q1–2024Q2, 2024Q4, 2025Q1–2025Q2 are final; 2024Q3 is missing (state did not submit) and 2025Q3–2025Q4 are provisional (93% and 70% of expected claims) and were excluded from all comparisons.
Exenatide rows are suppressed (count <11) in every quarter and were treated as unknown, never as zero; the suppressed volume is too small to change the direction of the findings.

arguments.summary: Yes — federal Medicaid DUR rules require screening of every prescription before it is filled or delivered. 42 CFR 456.705(b) obliges the State plan to provide for point-of-sale or point-of-distribution review of drug therapy using predetermined standards before each prescription is filled or delivered, and the review must screen for seven specified drug therapy problems. Technically the duty runs to the state (via the State plan), which must give pharmacies detailed compliance instructions that pharmacies must pass to their pharmacists; limited exemptions apply for certain nursing facility residents and for hospital-formulary and HMO-dispensed outpatient drugs.

findings.statement: Federal rule requires prospective review before dispensing: the State plan must provide for point-of-sale or point-of-distribution review of drug therapy using predetermined standards before each prescription is filled or delivered to the beneficiary or caregiver. [42-CFR-456.705(b)]

42 CFR 456.705(a) frames the requirement as a review of drug therapy before each prescription is filled or delivered, and requires the State to give pharmacies detailed information on what they must do to comply with prospective DUR (guidelines on counseling, profiling, and documentation), which pharmacies must in turn give to their pharmacists; standards for beneficiary/caregiver counseling come from applicable State law (including State Board policy incorporated by reference). [42-CFR-456.705(a)]

The screening must identify seven types of potential drug therapy problems: (1) therapeutic duplication (two or more drugs from the same therapeutic class where combined daily dose risks an adverse medical result or incurs added program cost without added therapeutic benefit); (2) drug-disease contraindication; (3) adverse drug-drug interaction; (4) incorrect drug dosage (a dosage outside the daily dosage in the predetermined standards; dosage = strength x quantity dispensed / day's supply); (5) incorrect duration of drug treatment (days of therapy exceeding or falling short of the predetermined standards); (6) drug-allergy interactions; and (7) clinical abuse/misuse. [42-CFR-456.705(b), 42-CFR-456.705(b)-2]
The DUR program must assess drug use information against predetermined standards; the screening is thus standards-based rather than purely pharmacist-discretionary. [42-CFR-456.703(d)]

Two exemptions narrow the requirement: prospective and retrospective DUR are not required for drugs dispensed to residents of nursing facilities that comply with the drug regimen review procedures in 42 CFR part 483 (states may still elect to apply it); and covered outpatient drugs dispensed by a hospital using drug formulary systems and billed at no more than the hospital's purchasing cost, and drugs dispensed by health maintenance organizations, are not subject to these subpart requirements. [42-CFR-456.703(b), 42-CFR-456.703(c)]

Separate prospective safety-edit/surveillance requirements address opioids: states must operate prospective safety edits (at state option in one case) or retrospective claims review to detect concurrent opioid plus benzodiazepine or antipsychotic prescribing, monitor antipsychotic use in children, and flag opioid prescribing to beneficiaries with opioid use disorder or on medication-assisted treatment, with possible co-prescribing of an opioid antagonist. [42-CFR-456.703(i)-2, 42-CFR-456.703(i)-3]

The parallel retrospective DUR rule confirms the same problem list is monitored after the fact (therapeutic appropriateness, over/underutilization, generic use, therapeutic duplication, drug-disease contraindication, drug-drug interaction, incorrect dosage, incorrect duration, clinical abuse/misuse), showing prospective screening targets the same categories. [42-CFR-456.709(b)]

The requirement is narrowed by limited exemptions, including that prospective and retrospective DUR are not required for drugs dispensed to residents of nursing facilities that comply with the drug regimen review procedures in 42 CFR part 483 (states may still elect to apply it), and for covered outpatient drugs dispensed through hospital drug formulary systems and certain HMO arrangements (42-CFR-456.705(c), 42-CFR-456.705(d)).

arguments.summary: Eastvale's GLP-1 prior authorization took effect 2024-07-01, not the May 15, 2024 announcement date (the bulletin's 2024-06-01 start was superseded by EV-BUL-2024-011, and the provider manual confirms July 1). Using that date, GLP-1 prescribing fell 18.6% in per-member rate (12.094 → 9.846 Rx per 1,000 member-months, 95% CI [-20.8%, -16.2%]) — a significant and material drop, with a sharp level shift at 2024Q3 rather than a pre-existing downward trend. Per-member GLP-1 spending fell 16.6% and the spending decomposition attributes essentially all of it to utilization per member (-18.4%), not price (+5.7%) or enrollment (-2.3%). This is a strong pre/post association, not proof of causation.

findings.statement: The authoritative effective date for EV's GLP-1 prior authorization is 2024-07-01 per the provider manual (EV-MAN-2024-PH), which supersedes the May 15, 2024 announcement (EV-BUL-2024-007, which had scheduled 2024-06-01) and is confirmed by EV-BUL-2024-011; claims with dates of service before July 1, 2024 require no PA. [EV-MAN-2024-PH#p1] [EV-BUL-2024-011#p1] [EV-BUL-2024-007#p1]

GLP-1 prescriptions per 1,000 member-months fell from a pre-period mean of 12.094 to a post-period mean of 9.846, a change of -18.6% (95% CI [-20.8%, -16.2%]) across 4 final pre quarters (2023Q3-2024Q2) and 4 final post quarters (2024Q3-2025Q2); verdict: significant_and_material at a 5% materiality threshold.
Per-member-per-month GLP-1 spending fell from $11.295 to $9.423, -16.6% (95% CI [-19.4%, -13.8%]), verdict significant_and_material.
Spending per prescription was essentially flat: $933.91 to $957.08, +2.5% (95% CI [1.0%, 4.0%]), verdict significant_but_immaterial — the volume decline, not price, drove the spending change.

Decomposing total GLP-1 spending from 2023Q3 ($17,006,544.62) to 2025Q2 ($14,343,494.48), -15.7%: utilization per member -18.4% (119.1% of the change), enrollment -2.3% (13.4%), and price per prescription +5.7% (-32.5%, i.e., offsetting). The decline is a utilization story, not a price or membership story.

The quarterly rate series shows a level shift at the policy boundary, not a pre-existing downward trend: 2023Q1-Q4 = 11.813, 12.064, 12.214, 11.751; 2024Q1 = 11.958; 2024Q2 = 12.450; then 2024Q3 = 9.792 and 2024Q4 = 10.047, holding at 9.571 (2025Q1) and 9.973 (2025Q2). The break appears in the first quarter after the July 1 effective date.

2024Q2, the policy-announced-but-not-yet-effective transition quarter, showed the highest per-member rate in the series (12.450), +3.45% over 2024Q1 (11.958), consistent with pre-mandate anticipatory prescribing; this cannot be separated from ordinary trend with quarterly data.

Six-month aggregates confirm the pattern with correct denominators: 2023H2 = 11.984, 2024H1 = 12.204 (rising into the policy), 2024H2 = 9.919, 2025H1 = 9.771 — the drop coincides with the first post-effective half-year.

Date-choice sensitivity: breaking at the 2024-05-15 announcement or the superseded 2024-06-01 date yields -17.9% (95% CI [-19.8%, -16.1%]), significant_and_material, with 2024Q2 excluded as a mixed quarter. The direction and magnitude are robust to which of the three dates is used at quarterly granularity.

2025Q3 and 2025Q4 are PROVISIONAL (claims run-out ~93% and ~70% complete) and were excluded from all comparisons; their lower apparent rates (8.744 and 6.787) are a claims-lag artifact, not evidence of a further decline.

Data suppression is balanced across periods: exactly 1 suppressed row per quarter in all 12 quarters, including every pre-period quarter, so suppression cannot manufacture the observed trend; unsuppressed prescription counts range 14,257-18,508 per quarter.

arguments.confidence_reason: The descriptive result is robust: all three metrics point one way, the CI excludes zero by a wide margin, the quarterly series shows a clean level shift coincident with the authoritative effective date rather than a pre-existing trend, the result survives using any of the three candidate dates, and suppression/denominator artifacts were checked and ruled out. Confidence in causation (as opposed to association) is lower and is called out in the caveats.
caveats: Pre/post association only — no control state or comparison series was used, so market-wide GLP-1 dynamics, benefit-design changes, manufacturer pricing, or media attention could contribute. Do not read this as a causal effect size.

The May 15, 2024 date was an ANNOUNCEMENT, not an effective date. It is not used as the policy start; because quarterly data cannot split mid-quarter, the -18.6% headline cannot isolate any anticipatory effect from the mandate itself.

2024Q2 is treated as a transition quarter (announced but not yet effective; only the final 10 days fall under the mandate). At quarterly granularity it is used as pre in E5 and excluded in E12/E13; that choice shifts the estimate by under 1 percentage point.
Only 4 final pre and 4 final post quarters exist, so the bootstrap CI rests on small n per side and is coarser than a true time-series confidence interval.

The decline could reflect fewer PA-eligible new starts, discontinuations, or switching to non-GLP1 classes; the data cannot distinguish these, and cross-class substitution (e.g., to SGLT2/insulin) was not tested here.
Two 2025 quarters are provisional (up to 30% of claims outstanding) and were excluded; any post-2025Q2 conclusions would be premature.

Internal QC note: an earlier aggregate query (E15) double-counted member-months through a join fan-out and produced inflated-low rates (pre 2.996, post 2.480). It was recomputed with correctly aggregated subqueries in E16 and must not be used.

arguments.summary: Yes — Northland GLP-1 spending per member per month rose sharply after the weight-management coverage: +42.4% (95% CI 40.1–44.6%) using the authoritative 2024-01-01 effective date, and +42.6% (40.2–45.0%) under the disputed 2024-02-01 manual date, so the result is not sensitive to the break-point choice. The driver was utilization per member, not membership or price: a 2023Q4→2025Q2 decomposition attributes 89.3% of the +40.4% total spending change to use per member (+35.4%), only 12.5% to price per prescription (+4.3%) and −1.8% to enrollment (−0.6%), with a longer 2023Q1→2025Q2 window giving the same ordering (80.4% utilization, 18.7% price, 0.9% enrollment). Price per prescription is statistically significant but immaterial (+2.6%, CI 1.3–4.0%). Two caveats matter: the data cannot be split by indication, so this is a population-expansion-consistent association, not proof the new BMI cohort caused it; and 2025Q3–Q4 are provisional/claims-lag and were excluded.

findings.statement: Northland GLP-1 reimbursement per member per month rose 42.4% (pre mean $10.889 → post mean $15.503 per member-month; 95% CI on the % change 40.1–44.6), verdict significant_and_material at a 5% materiality threshold, using the authoritative SPA effective date 2024-01-01; pre = 2023Q1–Q4, post = 2024Q1–Q4, no quarters excluded.

The finding is robust to the disclosed date conflict: rerunning with the pharmacy manual's 2024-02-01 date (2024Q1 treated as mixed and excluded, post = 2024Q2–2025Q1) gives +42.6% (95% CI 40.2–45.0), still significant_and_material.

Utilization per member rose materially: GLP-1 prescriptions per 1,000 member-months +38.8% (pre 11.834 → post 16.420; CI 36.4–41.0), significant_and_material; under the 2024-02-01 break point +37.8% (CI 35.8–39.6).

Price per prescription moved only slightly and did not clear the materiality bar: spend per Rx +2.6% (pre $920.165 → post $944.165; CI 1.3–4.0), verdict significant_but_immaterial; under the alternate date +3.5% (CI 1.8–5.2), verdict unchanged.

Spending decomposition 2023Q4→2025Q2: total GLP-1 spending +40.4% ($9,943,049.89 → $13,961,511.26); components are utilization per member +35.4%, price per Rx +4.3%, enrollment −0.6%, i.e. shares of the change of 89.3% utilization, 12.5% price, −1.8% enrollment.

The ordering holds over a wider window: 2023Q1→2025Q2 total spending +41.5% ($9,866,906.79 → $13,961,511.26) decomposes into utilization per member +32.2% (80.4% of the change), price per Rx +6.7% (18.7%) and enrollment +0.3% (0.9%).

Quarterly levels show the step at the policy boundary, not a trend in membership: member-months were essentially flat from 2023Q4 (903,358) to 2024Q1 (904,490), −0.62%, while GLP-1 spending rose 42.44% ($9,943,049.89 → $14,163,078.69) and prescriptions rose 41.32% (10,670 → 15,079).

The increase is broad across products rather than a mix shift: 2023Q4→2024Q1 prescriptions rose 41.33% for dulaglutide (3,201 → 4,524), 41.33% for liraglutide (1,067 → 1,508) and 41.32% for semaglutide (6,402 → 9,047), while supply price per unit rose only 4.33% ($232.97 → $243.06).

Data coverage: only final quarters were used (2023Q1–2025Q2); 2025Q3 and 2025Q4 are provisional (claims lag) and excluded — the 2025Q4 dip (spend per member-month $11,542.13, prescriptions 10,353) is a lag artifact, not a real decline. 12 rows are privacy-suppressed (exenatide in all 12 quarters), so an unknown but small volume is missing from the totals.

arguments.confidence_reason: All numbers come from final-quarter tool outputs and the direction/magnitude is insensitive to the 2024-01-01 vs 2024-02-01 break-point conflict, so the arithmetic and data-quality confidence is high. Confidence is lowered to medium because attribution is the weak link: the utilization files carry no indication field, there is no comparison state/control in this analysis, and exenatide is suppressed in every quarter.
caveats: Pre/post association only — no control group or interruption model was run, so this is consistent with, but does not prove, a policy effect (the tool itself warns pre/post does not establish causation).

GLP-1 claims cannot be segmented by indication, so the increase cannot be confirmed as coming from the new BMI≥30 / BMI≥27+comorbidity population rather than the unchanged type 2 diabetes population; the uniform ~41% rise across three different products is consistent with a broad new covered population but is not proof.
Policy text provides nothing on net price or rebates; the small price-per-Rx movement here is gross reimbursement and ignores any supplemental rebates, so net price effect is unknown.
Break-point conflict disclosed: primary analysis uses the authoritative 2024-01-01 SPA date; the pharmacy manual's 2024-02-01 date yields essentially identical results (42.6% vs 42.4%).
2025Q3–Q4 are provisional and excluded; the apparent Q4 drop is claims lag.
12 suppressed (privacy <11) rows, all exenatide, are NULL and were never treated as zero; magnitudes are small but the totals understate actual volume by an unknown amount.

arguments.summary: No — Southport's GLP-1 prescription counts grew only because enrollment grew. Comparing the final quarters available in both years (2023Q1, Q2, Q4 vs 2024Q1, Q2, Q4; 2024Q3 is missing), total GLP-1 prescriptions rose 6.2% (21,528 → 22,863) and member-months rose 6.2% (1,796,940 → 1,908,197), leaving the per-member fill rate essentially unchanged at 11.98 per 1,000 member-months in both years. The pre/post test on prescriptions per 1,000 member-months gives +0.4% with 95% CI [-3.0%, +3.9%] — verdict "no meaningful change". Units per prescription were a flat 4.0 in every quarter, so there is no sign of larger/longer fills either, and spending decomposition shows the 12.9% spending increase from 2023Q1 to 2024Q4 came from enrollment (+10.4%) and price per Rx (+5.0%), with utilization per member slightly negative (-2.6%).

findings.statement: Southport GLP-1 total prescriptions in the comparable final quarters (Q1, Q2, Q4) rose from 21,528 in 2023 to 22,863 in 2024 (+6.2%), while member-months rose from 1,796,940 to 1,908,197 (+6.19%), so prescriptions per 1,000 member-months were identical at 11.98 in both years.

Pre/post analysis of GLP-1 prescriptions per 1,000 member-months around 2024-01-01: pre mean 11.938, post mean 11.989, +0.4% change, 95% CI [-3.0%, +3.9%], below the 5% materiality threshold — verdict: no_meaningful_change (2024Q3 excluded as missing; 7 suppressed rows in window).

Utilization intensity per fill did not increase: units per prescription were exactly 4.0 in every final quarter 2023Q1–2024Q4, and total units also rose just 4.65% (29,688 → 31,068) from 2023Q4 to 2024Q4.

Quarterly per-member utilization was flat-to-down through 2024: 12.01 (2023Q1), 11.55 (2023Q2), 12.37 (2023Q4), 12.31 (2024Q1), 11.97 (2024Q2), 11.69 (2024Q4) prescriptions per 1,000 member-months, even as raw counts rose 4.8%, 9.3% and 4.6% year-over-year in those quarters.

Spending decomposition 2023Q1 → 2024Q4: total GLP-1 spending +12.9% ($6,590,667.34 → $7,442,694.42), driven by enrollment +10.4% and price per Rx +5.0%, offset by utilization per member -2.6% (shares of change: enrollment 81.7%, price 40.4%, utilization -22.1%).

Reimbursement per member per month rose 3.6% (pre mean $10.938 vs post mean $11.329), 95% CI [1.1%, 6.2%] — statistically detectable but below the 5% materiality threshold; verdict significant_but_immaterial.
